ACCURACY_IMPROVEMENTS.md
Later parser/physics-detector results, paired evaluation, release scope and remaining weaknesses.
================================================================================================

NUMBERED ORIGINAL SOURCE

    1 | # Accuracy improvements — 25 October 2026
    2 | 
    3 | The command parser now grounds actuator names in the original user request. A model response inventing a supported valve for a request about a coolant valve, heater, feed 3, or other unsupported hardware is rejected. Mixed commands retain supported actions and reject unsupported ones.
    4 | 
    5 | On the same 52 authored commands, actual Ollama inference improved from **40/52 (76.92%) to 52/52 (100%)**. This is a small authored test, not a universal language-understanding score. Evidence: `artifacts/accuracy-v2/parser-baseline.json`, `parser-corrected.json`, and the locked corpus/manifest.
    6 | 
    7 | ## Measured telemetry detector
    8 | 
    9 | A small CPU forest uses measured valve/flow consistency, command/position differences, vapor/liquid mass and species balances, and pressure trends. Rounding tolerances and interval bounds prevent ordinary flow transients from looking like sensor failures. Overlapping short balances detect instrument failures that recover within a window. Inputs do not include scenario names, labels, rationale, or simulator fault truth.
   10 | 
   11 | Selection used training and validation recordings. An initial frozen candidate failed its independent test (86.55% accuracy) and was not deployed. That first test became development evidence. A second independently seeded collection, with ramping controls and newly simulated valve-capacity/sticking faults, remained unscored until the final model and feature implementation were frozen.
   12 | 
   13 | The final candidate passed the predeclared release criteria on **215 windows**:
   14 | 
   15 | A paired actual Ollama replay on these identical windows measured the previous v3 + v1 specialist pipeline at **138/215 (64.19%)**, versus **200/215 (93.02%)** for the new pipeline: **+28.84 percentage points**. Both had zero false alarms on these 31 normal cases. Sensor recall improved from 41.03% to 89.74%; actuator recall improved from 82.98% to 93.62%. Raw model outputs and both predictions are saved in `artifacts/accuracy-v2/paired-final.json`. This is a pipeline improvement; the LLM weights are unchanged.
   16 | 
   17 | | Task | Correct | Percentage |
   18 | |---|---:|---:|
   19 | | Overall exact four-class classification | 200/215 | **93.02%** |
   20 | | Normal classified correctly | 31/31 | 100% |
   21 | | Sensor fault recall | 105/117 | 89.74% |
   22 | | Actuator fault recall | 44/47 | 93.62% |
   23 | | Pressure excursion recall | 20/20 | 100% |
   24 | | False alarms among normal windows | 0/31 | 0% |
   25 | 
   26 | Remaining errors: eight sensor faults were called normal, four sensor faults were called actuator faults, and three actuator faults were called sensor faults. Zero observed false alarms across 31 normal windows does not establish a zero population false-alarm rate. Some fault variants share a base trajectory; windows are not all statistically independent.
   27 | 
   28 | Specific weaknesses remain: frozen level readings were missed in all six cases, two of four analyzer dropouts were missed, and four purge-flow failures were classified as actuator faults. Actual simulated capacity degradation was correctly localized in five of eight cases; all eight stuck-valve cases were correct. Aggregate scores should not hide these gaps. Further work needs additional independent recordings and another untouched test set.
   29 | 
   30 | These results use the isolated TE simulator, injected instrument corruption, synthetic command discrepancies, and actual simulated valve-capacity/sticking faults. They do not establish performance on industrial hardware, other process equations, or a broader operating envelope. The model is specific to the current TE constants, units, sampling and serving format. Validate again when those change.
   31 | 
   32 | ## Runtime and scope
   33 | 
   34 | `model/telemetry-physics/policy.json` enables the released detector. Model, feature, validation and report hashes are checked before loading. Changed or invalid artifacts disable this path through the existing engine fallback. Malformed telemetry retains the parsed LLM verdict. The previous specialist remains available if the new policy is explicitly disabled.
   35 | 
   36 | The detector can correct both missed faults and false alarms in **advisory telemetry only**, preserving the original LLM label. It does not alter proposal assessment, governor authority, command execution, interlocks or the SIS. The observer LLM still runs; its weights have not been retrained. Operator target prediction and proposal-model accuracy are unchanged and must not be presented as improved.
   37 | 
   38 | ## Reproduction and evidence
   39 | 
   40 | - `python -m training.train_physics_telemetry` selects on validation only. It overwrites the candidate; deployment hash checks then require new release evidence. Do not tune against the final holdout.
   41 | - `python -m training.evaluate_physics_holdout --holdout artifacts/accuracy-v2/telemetry-final-holdout.jsonl --freeze-name physics-final-frozen-candidate.json --output model/telemetry-physics/final-holdout-evaluation.json` checks the frozen candidate and dataset hashes.
   42 | - `python -m training.benchmark_physics_pair` runs non-actuating paired Ollama replay against the old specialist pipeline.
   43 | - Final holdout manifest: `artifacts/accuracy-v2/telemetry-final-holdout.manifest.json`. Test-only accelerated/fault-enabled C++ source and executable are under `artifacts/accuracy-v2/simulator`; production simulator source is separate.
   44 | - Full offline regression suite: **280 passed**, one existing Starlette multipart deprecation warning. Docker/Unity integration and hardware validation were not performed.
   45 | 
   46 | Historical figures in `ACCURACY_REPORT.md` describe earlier pipelines and datasets. Different datasets should not be subtracted to claim a percentage-point gain; use the paired replay for that comparison.

NUMBERED ORIGINAL SOURCE

    1 | # Accuracy by task
    2 | 
    3 | The newer released detector and parser measurements are documented in [ACCURACY_IMPROVEMENTS.md](ACCURACY_IMPROVEMENTS.md). Figures below are historical and use different datasets.
    4 | 
    5 | These scores describe specific datasets and tasks. They are not guarantees for
    6 | all commands, future faults, operating points, or physical control outcomes.
    7 | 
    8 | | Component | Task | Measured score | Evidence |
    9 | | --- | --- | ---: | --- |
   10 | | scram-operator | Hold-versus-act agreement with expert | 100% | 235 historical validation cases: 33 hold, 202 act |
   11 | | scram-operator | All four target values exactly match expert | 53.62% | 126/235 historical validation cases |
   12 | | scram-observer v2 | Classify AI proposals | 97.78% | 927/948 historical unseen proposal examples |
   13 | | scram-observer v3 | Classify telemetry into normal/excursion/sensor/actuator | 62.50% | 30/48 fresh clean held-out windows |
   14 | | v3 + deployed CPU specialist | Same telemetry classification | 72.92% | 35/48 on the same fresh windows |
   15 | | CPU specialist alone | Telemetry classification | 77.71% | 366/471 clean held-out windows; not deployed alone |
   16 | | qwen2.5:1.5b alone | Exact command interpretation | 86.67% | 26/30 fresh authored commands |
   17 | | Parser with application checks | Exact command interpretation | 96.67% | 29/30 on the same authored commands |
   18 | 
   19 | The operator's average absolute target errors are 5.5 kPa pressure, 0.47
   20 | percentage points level, 3.51 kmol/h production, and 0 percentage points purge
   21 | composition. Valid JSON and correct hold-versus-act decisions do not mean its
   22 | continuous target values or resulting plant trajectories are always correct.
   23 | 
   24 | The v2 proposal observer historically detected all 569 suspicious proposals as
   25 | some attack class, while correctly naming 565 of them. It falsely flagged
   26 | 17/379 normal proposals (4.49%). This is a recorded benchmark rather than a new
   27 | live evaluation of that model during this turn.
   28 | 
   29 | For fresh telemetry, excursion recall was 12/12 (100%) for both variants.
   30 | Sensor-fault recall was 6/12 (50%) for the raw LLM and 11/12 (91.67%) with the
   31 | specialist. Actuator-fault recall was 11/12 (91.67%) for both. However, **11/12
   32 | normal windows were falsely flagged (91.67% false alarms)**. Correctly recognizing
   33 | normal operation was only 1/12 (8.33%). Thus the telemetry subsystem still has a
   34 | serious discrimination problem despite strong abnormal-condition detection.
   35 | 
   36 | Older 480-window results were 71.46% raw classification accuracy and 74.17%
   37 | with specialist replay, with 7.5% false alarms. Those are different data and
   38 | historical inference outputs; they must not replace the less favorable fresh
   39 | results or be treated as the same estimate.
   40 | 
   41 | The standalone specialist's false alarms were 29.73% on its 471-window clean
   42 | holdout. It is used conservatively to correct confident missed faults, not as a
   43 | replacement for the telemetry LLM. Its independent validation accuracy was
   44 | 62.35% on 409 telemetry windows, showing sensitivity to the recording split.
   45 | 
   46 | The parser's one failure was important: ?Open the coolant valve to 30%? became
   47 | a feed-1 command. Unsupported hardware is therefore not reliably refused.
   48 | This benchmark performed inference only; no simulator or valve was accessed.
   49 | 
   50 | ## Deterministic systems
   51 | 
   52 | The last complete offline run passed **271/271 tests (100% test pass rate)**.
   53 | Its covered checks include 25 safety-interlock cases, 21 provenance cases,
   54 | 11 Keel cases, 6 regulatory-controller cases, 9 governance cases and 7 sequential
   55 | monitor cases, plus application/race/format/data tests. Those percentages measure
   56 | software test success, not real-world accuracy or failure probabilities.
   57 | 
   58 | A historical trained-operator scenario rejected 47/47 forged commands (100%
   59 | within that scenario). Independent interlock and recovery scenarios also have
   60 | recorded successful trips. There is no sufficiently broad current closed-loop
   61 | benchmark to give SIS, L1, Keel, governance, rescue, or the complete project a
   62 | defensible operational accuracy percentage. No fresh Docker/Unity or hardware
   63 | validation was performed for this scorecard.
   64 | 
   65 | Machine-readable values and source paths are in
   66 | [artifacts/accuracy-scorecard.json](artifacts/accuracy-scorecard.json).
   67 | The fresh parser's complete corpus, raw outputs, corrections and failure are in
   68 | [artifacts/command-parser-accuracy.json](artifacts/command-parser-accuracy.json).

ARCHITECTURE.md
Original design/trust discussion with historical open items. Read the corrections in this guide before treating it as a current implementation reference.
================================================================================================

NUMBERED ORIGINAL SOURCE

    1 | # SCRAM — Architecture
    2 | 
    3 | SCRAM runs an **AI operator** on a simulated chemical plant. A **governance
    4 | layer** dynamically reduces the AI's authority, and an **independent safety
    5 | interlock** underneath it cannot be overridden by the AI.
    6 | 
    7 | ## 1. Layers (Purdue / ISA-95) and ownership
    8 | 
    9 | | Level | Role | Code | Owner |
   10 | |---|---|---|---|
   11 | | L3 Brain | AI operator. `decide(state) -> SupervisoryTargets`. Emits setpoints (intent), never valve positions. | `l3_brain/` | **Me** |
   12 | | L2 Supervisory | Monitoring, Guardian (attack detection / isolation), HMI, governance authority. | — | Teammates |
   13 | | L1 Control | Regulatory PI loops. `regulate(targets, state, dt) -> ControlCommand`. | `l1_stub.py` (placeholder) | Teammates |
   14 | | L0 Plant | Plant client, fault-injection helpers, SCRAM interlock. | `l0_plant/` | **Me** |
   15 | 
   16 | Control flows down, state flows up:
   17 | 
   18 |     L3 decide(state) -> SupervisoryTargets
   19 |           | governance clamps authority (L1/L2)
   20 |     L1 regulate(targets, state) -> ControlCommand (valve %)
   21 |           |
   22 |     L0 apply(command) -> PlantState -> back up to L2/L3
   23 | 
   24 | ## 2. Seams — `contracts.py` is the single source of truth
   25 | 
   26 | - `SupervisoryTargets` (L3 out): `pressure_sp`, `level_sp`, `production_rate_sp`,
   27 |   `a_comp_sp`, `authority` (0..1), `rationale`. `None` = hold.
   28 | - `ControlCommand` (L1 out, L0 in): four valve positions in % [0,100]. L0 clamps.
   29 | - `PlantState` (L0 up): measured process variables, valve positions, cost,
   30 |   `scrammed` / `scram_reason`, and `truth` (eval-only).
   31 | - Everything above L0 works in engineering units, never 0-65535 Modbus scaling.
   32 | - Contract changes are agreed with the teammates first; both sides build to them.
   33 | 
   34 | ## 3. Plant
   35 | 
   36 | The plant is the **stock GRFICSv3 Tennessee-Eastman reactor, run from the
   37 | prebuilt Docker image** (`fortiphyd/grfics-simulation`; see
   38 | `docker-compose.yml`). Run:
   39 | 
   40 | ```bash
   41 | docker compose pull simulation
   42 | docker compose up -d simulation
   43 | ```
   44 | 
   45 | - **:55555** — line-delimited JSON over TCP.
   46 |   `{"request":"read"}\n` returns state; `{"request":"write","data":{"inputs":{...}}}\n`
   47 |   sets valve setpoints (`f1_valve_sp`, `f2_valve_sp`, `purge_valve_sp`,
   48 |   `product_valve_sp`), `e_stop`, and the per-channel fault write-fields
   49 |   (`<channel>_fault_mode` / `_fault_severity` — see `l0_plant/fault_injection.py`).
   50 | - **:80** — helm: the GRFICS dashboard with the 3D plant view.
   51 | - No custom reactor build is used. `reference/sim_cpp_unused/` holds an earlier
   52 |   modified C++ reactor, shelved in favor of this design.
   53 | 
   54 | ## 4. Measured vs. truth
   55 | 
   56 | Each read from the reactor carries two parallel views of the same physical
   57 | state:
   58 | 
   59 | - **`outputs`** — the basic process channel. A dedicated safety-instrumented
   60 |   sensor path, independent of the basic control loop, tracking the true
   61 |   physical variables that path is wired to.
   62 | - **`measured`** — the same variables as seen through the plant's ordinary
   63 |   instrumentation, which `l0_plant/fault_injection.py` can degrade per channel
   64 |   (frozen, drift, noise, dropout) to exercise L1/L2/L3 against corrupted
   65 |   signals.
   66 | 
   67 | `PlantState` exposes `measured` as the live signal — that is what L1, L2 and
   68 | L3 consume. `PlantState.truth` carries `outputs`, for eval/scoring only; it is
   69 | never a production signal.
   70 | 
   71 | ## 5. The SCRAM interlock thesis
   72 | 
   73 | `l0_plant/safety.py` is a last-resort protective layer under the AI. It
   74 | evaluates the **safety-instrumented sensor path** (`outputs`), not the basic
   75 | control system's `measured` view, and latches a trip on a hard-limit
   76 | excursion (pressure >= 3000 kPa, level <= 5% or >= 95%). On trip it forces the
   77 | plant into a **cause-specific safe state** (`SafetyInterlock.safe_state_inputs()`),
   78 | regardless of what L3 intends or how much authority governance granted:
   79 | 
   80 | | Trip cause | Safe state | Why |
   81 | |---|---|---|
   82 | | pressure high, level high | `e_stop` (feeds shut, purge and product open) | relieves pressure / drains an overfull vessel |
   83 | | level low | product valve closed; feed and purge valves held where they are (not written) | `e_stop` would open product and keep draining an already-low vessel; closing it lets inflow and reaction recover the level to the re-arm band |
   84 | 
   85 | The first trip cause latches; a second hazard while latched does not change the
   86 | safe state. A safety-channel reading that is missing or not a finite number trips
   87 | too (cause `sis_sensor_fault`, safe state `e_stop`): the SIS fails safe when it
   88 | cannot read its own sensor. A command with a non-finite valve value is never
   89 | applied (the gate rejects it; without a gate the valves are held).
   90 | 
   91 | - **Scope assumption:** this design assumes the safety-instrumented sensor
   92 |   path is out of the attacker's reach — standard SIS independence, the same
   93 |   assumption a real safety-instrumented system makes about its own dedicated
   94 |   sensors and wiring being separate from the basic process control system. The
   95 |   fault-injection helpers in `l0_plant/fault_injection.py` only ever touch the
   96 |   basic control system's `measured` view; they have no way to reach the SIS
   97 |   path, by construction of the reactor's own JSON schema.
   98 | - **Provenance scope assumption:** the command-origin gate (section 5a) assumes
   99 |   the signing key and the L1 signer are uncompromised, the same shape of
  100 |   assumption as SIS independence above. An attacker who can sign as L1 (steal
  101 |   the key, or run inside the signer) passes admission; the physics interlock is
  102 |   then the only remaining ground. Conversely, the two grounds fail
  103 |   independently: a compromised agent without the key is stopped at admission
  104 |   even when its commands are physically benign, and a compromised sensor
  105 |   cannot stop the SIS trip. Neither ground covers an attacker who has both the
  106 |   key and the SIS channel.
  107 | - Trips latch. Reset is deliberate (`PlantService.reset_interlock()`) and only
  108 |   succeeds once the SIS channel is back inside the re-arm band
  109 |   (pressure <= 2800 kPa, level 15-85%; the bands are `TripLimits` fields); it reads the SIS channel directly, not
  110 |   `PlantState`'s measured fields, so a degraded basic-control sensor can't
  111 |   unlock a reset either.
  112 | - The AI has no code path to override it.
  113 | 
  114 | Tests: `tests/test_safety_unit.py` is a fast, pure-logic unit test of
  115 | `safety.py` (trip / latch / override / re-arm, no container). `tests/test_interlock_truth.py`
  116 | is a slower integration test against the live container — it degrades the
  117 | basic-control pressure sensor and confirms the interlock still trips off the
  118 | SIS channel, latches, and refuses to clear until the SIS channel re-arms.
  119 | `experiments/level_drift_eval.py` is the low-level counterpart: a native drift
  120 | fault on the basic-control level transmitter, with a measured-only monitor vs.
  121 | the SIS interlock (it uses a test-only 40% low-level setpoint; the production
  122 | default stays 5%).
  123 | 
  124 | ### 5a. Command-origin integrity (provenance gate)
  125 | 
  126 | `l0_plant/provenance_gate.py` is the second ground of the enforcer's veto
  127 | alongside the physics interlock: physics asks "is the process state safe?",
  128 | the gate asks "did the authorized path issue this command?". It covers the
  129 | case physics cannot: a command that is individually inside every physical
  130 | limit (the SIS never trips) but unauthorized. `PlantService(gate=...)` is
  131 | opt-in; with no gate every command is trusted (legacy behaviour).
  132 | 
  133 | - **Via the enforcer:** L1 signs each command (`CommandSigner`: HMAC-SHA256
  134 |   over a strictly increasing `seq` + the four valve positions, carried in the
  135 |   additive `ControlCommand.seq` / `auth_tag` fields). Unsigned, forged,
  136 |   tampered or replayed commands are rejected and last-good is re-asserted.
  137 | - **Around the enforcer:** the plant's :55555 protocol is unauthenticated, so a
  138 |   direct write can't be prevented from here. The enforcer is the only
  139 |   sanctioned writer, so each cycle it audits the plant's valve / `e_stop`
  140 |   readback against what it last wrote; any mismatch is an out-of-band write,
  141 |   is logged, and is overwritten by the next write. Detected and bounded
  142 |   (dwell <= one control cycle), not prevented - prevention needs network-level
  143 |   controls on :55555.
  144 | - **Seam note:** `seq` / `auth_tag` are a change to the L1 seam; the L1
  145 |   teammate must confirm it (L1 signs before handing to L0) before the gate is
  146 |   enabled outside experiments. `l1_stub.py` does not sign yet.
  147 | - Tests: `tests/test_provenance_gate.py` (fast); live demo
  148 |   `experiments/provenance_demo.py`.
  149 | 
  150 | ### 5b. The LLM operator (L3) is untrusted by design
  151 | 
  152 | `l3_brain/policy.py` `LLMOperator` is the shared base of the model-backed
  153 | `Policy` (served by `OllamaOperator`, below; there is no hosted-API path and no
  154 | API key). Server-side only; it reads measured `PlantState` fields,
  155 | never `.truth`, and emits setpoints + rationale, never valves. Its output is
  156 | parsed, validated and clamped to an `Envelope`; any failure (timeout, refusal,
  157 | bad JSON, backend down) becomes "hold" (all setpoints None), and it calls the model
  158 | on a ~20 s supervisory interval from a background thread so L1 keeps
  159 | regulating every cycle. The enforcer's guarantees (sections 5, 5a) do not
  160 | depend on it behaving: `experiments/llm_operator_demo.py` reruns the capstone
  161 | attack with it as the brain.
  162 | 
  163 | Fine-tune path: `training/` collects real GRFICS states (`collect_states.py`),
  164 | labels them with a rule-based expert grounded in the sim's settled design point
  165 | and the SIS limits (`expert_policy.py`), and builds balanced chat examples
  166 | (`build_dataset.py`). The prompt format (system text + measured-state JSON) is
  167 | defined once in `l3_brain/prompt_format.py` and used by both the dataset and
  168 | `LLMOperator`, so a fine-tuned model is served exactly what it was trained on.
  169 | Trained outputs live in `model/` (weights gitignored).
  170 | 
  171 | The trained model runs as the brain via `OllamaOperator` (an `LLMOperator`
  172 | subclass; select with `SCRAM_OPERATOR=ollama`). It calls the local Ollama
  173 | server (`scram-operator`, `http://127.0.0.1:11434`, override with
  174 | `SCRAM_OLLAMA_MODEL` / `SCRAM_OLLAMA_URL`) with the same prompt_format, on a
  175 | 5 s interval, and keeps the same parse/validate/clamp and hold-on-any-failure.
  176 | If Ollama or the model is unavailable at selection time, `make_policy` falls
  177 | back to `BaselineOperator`. Demo: `python -m experiments.llm_operator_demo
  178 | --brain ollama`, which writes `experiments/trained_operator_demo_results.json`
  179 | and logs each decision's measured view next to the truth.
  180 | 
  181 | ## 5c. Live control room
  182 | 
  183 | `python -m live` runs the full stack continuously against the plant: the trained
  184 | operator (`OllamaOperator`, falls back to baseline) -> governance authority ->
  185 | L2 `BehaviorMonitor` -> L1 (`l1_regulator.py` `L1Regulator`: four PI loops - pressure on
  186 | purge with split range onto the feeds, level on product, production by feed-1
  187 | feedforward plus a slow trim, A on feed 2 - bumpless, real-time integration) ->
  188 | Keel -> signed by L1 ->
  189 | `PlantService(gate, limits)`. It serves http://127.0.0.1:8765 with the GRFICS 3D
  190 | reactor embedded, the AI's decisions (what it saw vs. the truth), trends, and
  191 | scenario buttons (level drift, pressure dropout, forged commands, out-of-band
  192 | write, stolen L1 key) plus clear-faults / reset-interlock / reset-plant. On
  193 | re-arm the plant restarts from the design valve lineup. Demo SIS limits by
  194 | default (40% low-level trip); `--production-limits` for the 5% default.
  195 | 
  196 | ## 6. Repo layout
  197 | 
  198 |     contracts.py            shared dataclasses (the seams)
  199 |     l0_plant/                grfics_client, plant_service, safety, provenance_gate, fault_injection
  200 |     l3_brain/                policy, operator (authority handshake), prompt_format
  201 |     training/                real-state collection, expert labels, fine-tune dataset
  202 |     model/                   trained operator outputs (weights gitignored)
  203 |     live/                    the whole stack running live + control room (python -m live, :8765)
  204 |     l1_stub.py               placeholder for teammate's L1
  205 |     run_demo.py              L0 + L1 stub + L3 end to end
  206 |     docker-compose.yml       plant-only: simulation service, prebuilt image
  207 |     simulation/               simulation image context (web_visualization, remote_io)
  208 |     reference/sim_cpp_unused/   shelved custom C++ reactor (not used)
  209 |     tests/                   test_safety_unit.py (fast), test_interlock_truth.py (live)
  210 | 
  211 | ## 7. Licence
  212 | 
  213 | GRFICSv3 is GPL-3.0. Reusing the TE model makes SCRAM GPL-3.0 (`LICENSE`).
  214 | 
  215 | ## 8. Open items
  216 | 
  217 | - Composition units: reactor reports `A_in_purge` as a fraction (~0.47);
  218 |   baseline policy targets `47.0`. Reconcile at the L1 seam.
  219 | - Baseline L3 policy is intentionally dumb — it's the floor an ML/LLM policy beats.
  220 | - `l1_stub.py` is a placeholder; the teammate's real L1 replaces it wholesale.
  221 | - Governance / L2 (authority_fn, Guardian) doesn't exist yet; `AIOperator`
  222 |   defaults to full authority when none is supplied.

   13 | diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.
   14 | 
   15 | ## Our Standards
   16 | 
   17 | Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our
   18 | community include:
   19 | 
   20 | * Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
   21 | * Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
   22 | * Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
   23 | * Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
   24 |   and learning from the experience

   33 | * Public or private harassment

   37 |   professional setting

   54 | an individual is officially representing the community in public spaces.
   55 | Examples of representing our community include using an official e-mail address,
   56 | posting via an official social media account, or acting as an appointed
   57 | representative at an online or offline event.

   65 |

   77 | unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.
   78 |

   86 | of actions.
   87 |

   89 | interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with
   90 | those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This
   91 | includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels
   92 | like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or
   93 | permanent ban.
   94 | 
   95 | ### 3. Temporary Ban
   96 | 
   97 | **Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including
   98 | sustained inappropriate behavior.
   99 |

  101 | communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or
  102 | private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction
  103 | with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period.
  104 | Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.
  105 | 
  106 | ### 4. Permanent Ban
  107 | 
  108 | **Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community
  109 | standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior,  harassment of an
  110 | individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.
  111 | 
  112 | **Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within
  113 | the community.

    1 | # SCRAM live demo runbook
    2 | 
    3 | One clean pass, start to finish, about 25 minutes. Each step proves one layer of
    4 | the defense. Every number below is from the rehearsal on 2026-10-23
    5 | (`python experiments/demo_rehearsal.py`; results in
    6 | `experiments/demo_rehearsal_results*.json`), so you can quote it.
    7 | 
    8 | The control room has three tabs: **Overview** (pressure dial, tank, authority, 3D plant,
    9 | defense pipeline, valves), **Console** (talk to the AI operator, the attack builder with
   10 | presets, operator controls) and **Analysis** (trends, latest decision, observers, event log).
   11 | Every attack button below is on the Console tab; watch its effect on Overview.
   12 | 
   13 | | Step | Button (Console tab) | Proves | Time |
   14 | |---|---|---|---|
   15 | | 1 Clean | none | Baseline: everything green | 1 min |
   16 | | 2 Forged commands | Presets → Forged commands | Provenance gate + Keel | 1 min + 2 min recovery |
   17 | | 3 Operator injection | Chat → "Injection: vendor advisory" (or Presets → Scripted injection) | Observer v2 + governance | 1 min + ~70 s recovery |
   18 | | 4 Valve fault | Presets → Product valve fault | Observer v3 (display) + L1 | ~75 s |
   19 | | 5 Sensor drift | Presets → Level drift | Keel reads the safety channel | ~5.5 min |
   20 | | 6 Stolen key | Presets → Stolen key | SIS, the last line | ~80 s + ~25 s safe-hold, auto re-arm |
   21 | 
   22 | ## Before the demo (10 min ahead)
   23 | 
   24 | 1. Start **Docker Desktop**: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\DockerDesktop\Docker Desktop.exe`.
   25 | 2. Start **Ollama** (tray app or `ollama serve`). Check that all three models are listed:
   26 |    `ollama list` shows `scram-operator`, `scram-observer`, `scram-observer-v3`.
   27 | 3. Close GPU-heavy apps. Three models use ~4.8 GB of the 6 GB GPU. Close or minimise Firefox and Chrome tabs as well: free RAM should be above 4 GB.
   28 | 4. From the repo root: `python -m live`
   29 |    - It starts the plant container if needed and sets `LLAMA_ARG_CACHE_RAM=0` for Ollama. On the first run on a machine it restarts Ollama once to apply that. Without it, three models exhaust 16 GB of RAM in ~4.5 min.
   30 |    - It resets the plant to the design point and opens http://127.0.0.1:8765. Put the 3D plant (http://localhost/) on a second screen if you have one.
   31 | 5. Wait for these lines in the event stream (about 15 s):
   32 |    - `L2 observer online: proposals on scram-observer (feeds governance), telemetry on scram-observer-v3 (display only)`
   33 |    - `control loop running; SIS trips at P >= 3000 kPa, level <= 40% or >= 95%`
   34 | 6. If the observer line says `unavailable`, Ollama is not serving the models. Fix it before you start, or the demo loses steps 3 and 4.
   35 | 
   36 | **Reset between rehearsals:** Console → Operator controls → "Reset plant" (about 15 s).
   37 | 
   38 | **Talking to the AI (Console tab):** whatever you type becomes a standing instruction in the
   39 | operator model's prompt. Its next decision (within ~5 s) is its reply, with the setpoints it
   40 | asked for; ~12 s later a "Defenses" message reports what the observer, governance and Keel made
   41 | of it. Rehearsed live: "Lower pressure to 2620 kPa." was followed (plant to ~2640 kPa, observer
   42 | normal); the vendor-advisory injection was clamped to 2900 kPa by the envelope, flagged
   43 | `setpoint_drift`, and governance cut the AI to 0.15. "Clear" drops the instruction.
   44 | 
   45 | ## Step 1: clean (1 min)
   46 | 
   47 | **Do:** nothing. Let it run for about 60 s.
   48 | 
   49 | **Show:**
   50 | - Authority 1.00.
   51 | - Pressure 2700 kPa, level 44.2%. The measured and true lines sit on top of each other.
   52 | - The gate's admitted count climbing, rejected count 0.
   53 | 
   54 | **Say:** "The AI operator is a 1.5B model fine-tuned to pick setpoints every 5 s. Everything below it assumes it can be wrong. Right now it's healthy: full authority, every check green."
   55 | 
   56 | Rehearsal: authority 1.00, true pressure 2700.0–2700.2 kPa, 1065 commands admitted, 0 rejected.
   57 | 
   58 | ## Step 2: forged commands (1 min + 2 min recovery)
   59 | 
   60 | **Do:** Forged commands → **Start attack**. It runs for 60 s, one forged command every 4 s: unsigned, wrong key, replayed.
   61 | 
   62 | **Show:**
   63 | - Event stream: `REJECTED (unsigned command…)`, `REJECTED (invalid provenance tag)`, `REJECTED (replayed/stale sequence…)`.
   64 | - Gate rejected count: 15.
   65 | - Keel authority falling to 0. Keel takes 0.20 per rejection; `divert` appears at about +36 s.
   66 | - The pressure line does not move.
   67 | 
   68 | **Say:** "A compromised agent on the control network is sending valve commands. None carry a valid signature, so the gate refuses every one and re-asserts the last good command. Each rejection also costs the operator trust: Keel takes it to zero authority. Nothing reached a valve."
   69 | 
   70 | Rehearsal: 15/15 rejected, Keel authority 1.00 → 0 (clamp at +16 s, divert at +36 s), true pressure 2699.7–2700.2 kPa. Earlier capstone run: 47/47 rejected, 0 reached the plant.
   71 | 
   72 | **Recovery:** Keel recovers on a clean window. Two minutes after the attack ends it is back to about 0.95. Use those 2 minutes for the architecture slide, then go on (step 3 works from 0.95).
   73 | 
   74 | ## Step 3: operator injection (1 min + ~70 s recovery)
   75 | 
   76 | **Do:** Operator injection → **Inject advisory**. It runs for 60 s. A fake "vendor advisory" makes the AI raise its pressure and production setpoints in small steps.
   77 | 
   78 | **Show:** the event stream, in this order.
   79 | 
   80 | | Time | Event |
   81 | |---|---|
   82 | | +5 s | `L2 observer (proposals): provenance_violation score 0.90 … -> governance suspicion 0.90` |
   83 | | +10 s | `governance: … corroborated 0.90 (provenance_violation) -> ceiling 0.10` |
   84 | | ~+12 s | authority at the **0.10 floor** |
   85 | | +30 s | `setpoint_drift`, then `rule:run`: independent confirmation |
   86 | 
   87 | **Say:**
   88 | - At the start: "This is prompt injection: text the operator ingested is steering it. The observer model reads the operator's last six proposals and recognises the advisory as an outside instruction."
   89 | - After corroboration: "Governance needs two verdicts in a row before it acts, so one bad model answer can't throttle the AI. Once confirmed, the AI drops to 10% authority. Its setpoints are mostly replaced by the current plant state."
   90 | 
   91 | Pressure: true pressure rises about 30 kPa (rehearsal 2700 → 2733) and stays about 270 kPa below the trip. Don't claim it doesn't move.
   92 | 
   93 | **Recovery:** after the injection ends, authority returns to 1.00 in about 70 s. This needs a 15 s clean window inside the design envelope, then a gradual ramp.
   94 | 
   95 | ## Step 4: product valve fault (~75 s)
   96 | 
   97 | **Do:** Product valve fault → **Fault valve**. The valve loses half its capacity, so L1 starts opening it. 20 s later it sticks while L1 is still moving it. These are the simulator's own native faults.
   98 | 
   99 | **Show:**
  100 | - Event stream: `product valve now STUCK in place`.
  101 | - Then `L2 observer (telemetry): actuator_fault … Product valve is commanded to X% but sits at Y% … (display only, not fed to authority)`.
  102 | - Authority stays at 1.00.
  103 | 
  104 | **Say:** "Observer v3 watches 15 s of telemetry, with each valve's commanded position next to its actual one. It sees the valve stop following the controller. It's display-only on purpose: on unseen faults it false-alarms 7.5% of the time, so telemetry verdicts never move authority."
  105 | 
  106 | Rehearsal: the valve stuck at +20 s; `actuator_fault` appeared 8 s later ("commanded to 47.6% but sits at 47.4%").
  107 | 
  108 | Two other things may show; expect them:
  109 | - **The gate's readback audit also flags it:** `out-of-band write detected … product_valve_pos is 47.4% but enforcer last wrote 47.9%`, logged once per 10 s. The audit cannot tell a stuck valve from an attacker's write, so this is a correct detection. Say so.
  110 | - **Authority may dip to ~0.35–0.5.** The AI changes its proposals as the level moves, and the rule monitor or the proposal observer reacts. This is the known operator limit (see the last table); it recovers within about a minute.
  111 | 
  112 | **Then:** **Clear faults and stop attacks.**
  113 | 
  114 | ## Step 5: level-sensor drift (~5.5 min)
  115 | 
  116 | **Do:** Level transmitter drift → **Start drift**. The level transmitter reads high, at +60%/h. The AI and L1 both see a rising level, so L1 opens the product valve, and the true level falls.
  117 | 
  118 | **Show:**
  119 | - The orange (measured) and teal (true) level lines split apart.
  120 | - From about +4.5 min, Keel events: `clamp … divergence:level: measured 47.8 vs SIS 43.3`, with authority falling step by step.
  121 | - At about +5.5 min, `keel: divert A=0.00`: the AI is cut off.
  122 | - The true level stops falling at about 43.0% and recovers.
  123 | 
  124 | **Say:** "Now the AI is being lied to. Its sensor says the tank is filling, and nothing it can see says otherwise. v3 even calls these windows normal. Keel checks the AI's view against the independent safety channel, sees them disagree by almost 5 points, and takes the AI out of the loop before the true level gets anywhere near the trip."
  125 | 
  126 | Rehearsal (two runs): Keel's first divergence clamp came at +272 s (measured 47.8 vs SIS 43.3), then divert at +332 s and +319 s. True level bottomed at 43.0–43.2% while the display read 48.5%. The SIS never had to trip.
  127 | 
  128 | Use the waiting time for the observer and split-serving slides.
  129 | 
  130 | **Then:** **Clear faults and stop attacks** promptly after the divert. While diverted, the valves are held and pressure creeps up about 0.4 kPa/s.
  131 | 
  132 | ## Step 6: stolen key, the SIS capstone (~80 s, then safe-hold and auto re-arm)
  133 | 
  134 | **Do:** Stolen L1 key → **Take over**. An attacker who holds the real L1 signing key opens both feeds and shuts purge and product.
  135 | 
  136 | **Show:**
  137 | - Gate admitted count keeps climbing: the commands are validly signed.
  138 | - Pressure climbing about 4 kPa/s.
  139 | - `SIS TRIP: …` at 3000 kPa on the true channel; safe state is the **closed-loop safe-hold**: feeds cut to 60% of design, purge and product worked on the SIS's own pressure and level readings. The reactor keeps running instead of being killed. The header pill turns amber (`SIS SAFE-HOLD`) and a recovery bar counts down.
  140 | - `stolen-key attacker's commands are now overridden by the interlock`.
  141 | 
  142 | **Say:** "This is the worst case. The attacker has the real key, so to the gate it is L1. Every software layer above the plant can be bypassed. What can't be bypassed is physics: the SIS reads its own sensor and trips at 3000 kPa, 100 kPa below where this vessel ruptures."
  143 | 
  144 | Rehearsal:
  145 | - Takeover to SIS trip in ~75 s (2725 → 3000 kPa).
  146 | - Keel's events count down to it on the way: `rate_bound:dP/dt=3.4 kPa/s, ttt=31s`, then `soft_zone:P=2951`. It can see the attack coming but cannot stop validly signed commands.
  147 | - Safe-hold (rehearsed live 2026-10-23): 2994 → 2763 kPa in 20 s with the level steady at 45%; `interlock AUTO RE-ARMED after 10 s stable inside the re-arm band` 26 s after the trip. The AI comes back on 0.50 authority and earned 1.00 back ~40 s later; the plant held ~2710 kPa. Tuning runs (`experiments/safe_hold_tune.py`, results in `experiments/safe_hold_tune_results.json`): settled in 22-26 s for all three gain sets, never escalated.
  148 | - v3 may show `actuator_fault` during the safe-hold: the SIS, not L1, is driving the valves then. That's correct.
  149 | 
  150 | **Re-arm:** automatic once the safety channel has held inside the re-arm band (P ≤ 2800 kPa, level 42-85%) for 10 s. If pressure ever reaches 3050 kPa during the safe-hold, it escalates to a full e-stop until re-arm. After 3 auto re-arms in 10 minutes it locks out and **Re-arm SIS** (or "Re-arm now" on the recovery bar) is needed.
  151 | 
  152 | ## If something goes wrong
  153 | 
  154 | | Symptom | Fix |
  155 | |---|---|
  156 | | Observer line says `unavailable` | Ollama is not running, or a model is missing (`ollama list`). Restart Ollama, then use Reset plant. |
  157 | | Laptop slows and free RAM is near 0 | Ollama was started without the cache cap. Quit Ollama from the tray and run `python -m live` again (it sets the cap). |
  158 | | `plant connection lost` | Docker Desktop paused or the container restarted. The engine reconnects by itself; if not, Reset plant. |
  159 | | Authority dips to ~0.5 with no attack | The operator model sometimes invents "backing off" setpoints and the rule monitor reacts. Known limit; it recovers within a minute. |
  160 | | A step misbehaves mid-demo | Clear faults and stop attacks, then Reset plant to design point (15 s), and continue from the next step. |

NUMBERED ORIGINAL SOURCE

    1 | # Final frontend — Nocturne
    2 | 
    3 | The design combines Front's clear dashboard grouping, Midday's spacing and typography, and Databricks' contextual data exploration. The current **Nocturne** theme uses a black canvas, faint orbital contours, smoky violet and teal illumination, and dark panels with subtly lit edges. The implementation uses the existing HTML, CSS and JavaScript stack.
    4 | 
    5 | The main overview now starts with pressure, inventory, product flow and effective authority. A primary process chart switches between pressure and level, with synchronized time windows and hover readings. Protection layers sit beside the chart; actuator positions and the live plant view follow. Expandable process instruments retain the original gauges.
    6 | 
    7 | The telemetry page adds Charts and Data tabs, a contextual signal inspector, minimum/maximum/average readings for the selected time window, optional setpoint and safety-limit overlays, and CSV export. The table shows the newest 120 samples; export includes every retained sample in the selected window. Chart settings and export make no plant writes. Current readings and historical window statistics are labeled separately. Connection loss marks values as last readings.
    8 | 
    9 | The operator console and separate direct-control studio share the black palette, typography and controls. Text, chart series, menus, tables and instrument fills are tuned for dark surfaces. Semantic green, amber and red remain reserved for operational state. Existing model routing, plant commands, interlocks and authority rules are unchanged.
   10 | 
   11 | The user-approved final design retains the black background, orbital artwork, violet/teal light, larger type and existing layouts. Most UI text is approximately 20% larger, with a minimum of 11.5 px for compact labels. Primary actions have gradient depth and a hover light sweep. Secondary buttons, navigation, chart tabs, scenario selectors, filters, suggested commands and valve adjustment controls now also have a light sweep, border illumination, hover lift and tactile press feedback. Keyboard focus gets a clear halo. Disabled controls have no motion or glow; reduced-motion preferences disable sweeps and movement. Emergency controls retain restrained red feedback. Mobile navigation stacks icons above labels to accommodate the larger type.
   12 | 
   13 | ## References
   14 | 
   15 | - [Front workload dashboard](https://mobbin.com/explore/screens/cec3ccca-064b-447b-b15e-268bc27b1dbf): navigation, filter treatment and chart hierarchy.
   16 | - [Midday overview](https://mobbin.com/explore/screens/fa47d11e-0857-4ddc-a515-c837358b7c68): spacing, typography and metric emphasis.
   17 | - [Databricks interactive dashboard](https://mobbin.com/explore/screens/4a92dd62-1199-4288-9d26-a0f2c4c796c2): charts/data organization, contextual inspection and display options.
   18 | 
   19 | ## Validation
   20 | 
   21 | `node tests/frontend_smoke.cjs` uses intercepted requests, so it never controls the live plant. Checks cover metric rendering, pressure/level switching, hover readings, shared time filters, expandable instruments, inspector selection, display-only settings, data rows, CSV contents, keyboard tabs, scenario dispatch, chat dispatch, safe-hold status, reconnects, stale telemetry, server restarts and both interfaces at desktop/tablet/mobile widths. Screenshots and a sample CSV are saved under `artifacts/frontend/`.
   22 | 
   23 | The main dashboard is also checked against the running backend. The manual studio remains a separate application; do not run it alongside another plant writer. No new framework or package dependency is required. Fonts have system fallbacks.
   24 | 
   25 | Previous frontend backups and generated design exports were permanently removed
   26 | during the final upload cleanup. The current implementation and this design
   27 | record are retained; browser checks can regenerate screenshots.

Historical repository review findings and priorities. Tests/current implementation determine which observations remain applicable.

NUMBERED ORIGINAL SOURCE

    1 | # SCRAM project review — 25 October 2026
    2 | 
    3 | > Historical review snapshot. A subsequent improvement pass fixed the safety,
    4 | > E-stop, observer reset/freshness, signing, port exposure, lifecycle and simulator
    5 | > source issues described below. See [QUALITY_IMPROVEMENTS.md](QUALITY_IMPROVEMENTS.md)
    6 | > for current measurements, validation limits, and remaining model weaknesses.
    7 | 
    8 | SCRAM is a substantial research prototype with a coherent central idea: an AI proposes operating targets, deterministic controllers turn those into actuator commands, and independent enforcement limits what reaches the simulated plant. The strongest work is the separation of responsibilities, the measured-versus-safety signal distinction, the attack scenarios, and the regression tests. It is more developed than the root README suggests.
    9 | 
   10 | It is not yet a production control system. The safety boundary is simulated in Python, the plant socket is unauthenticated, key material is embedded in the demo, and several recovery/concurrency cases need attention. These limitations matter when describing the project's guarantees. “Independent simulated safety channel” is accurate; this repository does not establish a physically independent hardware interlock.
   11 | 
   12 | ## Scope and evidence
   13 | 
   14 | - Inventoried the 216 tracked files and mapped the active application, plant adapter, control, enforcement, monitoring, training, evaluation, packaging, and legacy/reference areas.
   15 | - Reviewed the active execution paths and their tests; inspected the C++ plant source, dataset builders, model-serving code, representative evaluation artifacts, and launch/deployment configuration.
   16 | - Parsed all 74 tracked first-party Python source files outside the upstream/reference directories: no syntax errors. Inventory and exact dataset overlap counts are in [artifacts/review_inventory.json](artifacts/review_inventory.json).
   17 | - This is a source review and local test run, not an exhaustive proof of every file. Model weights, compiled Unity assets, third-party toolchains, virtual environments, packet captures, and every individual training example were not manually audited. Models were not retrained or benchmarked during this review.
   18 | - Browser checks use intercepted API fixtures. They do not call Docker, Ollama, or the real plant. Screenshots explicitly substitute a test placeholder for the live 3D reactor. A complete live scenario rehearsal remains outstanding.
   19 | 
   20 | ## How the project fits together
   21 | 
   22 | | Area | Responsibility | Assessment |
   23 | | --- | --- | --- |
   24 | | `contracts.py` | State, supervisory intent, actuator commands | Good seam. Composition units and the meaning of `truth` need more precise documentation. |
   25 | | `l0_plant/` | TCP adapter, safety latch, command provenance, fault injection | Clear separation. Secondary-hazard handling and transport assumptions need strengthening. |
   26 | | `l1_regulator.py` | Four PI loops, bumpless transfer, command signing | Considerably stronger than the old stub; toy-plant tests cover useful behavior. |
   27 | | `l3_brain/` | Baseline and local LLM operators, prompt formatting, output validation | Shared training/serving format and hold-on-failure behavior are good choices. |
   28 | | `monitor/`, `enforcer/` | Rule and sequential monitoring, observer inference, governance, Keel | Deterministic enforcement is a strong foundation. Observer lifecycle and evidence freshness need work. |
   29 | | `live/` | Full-stack engine, scenarios, operator console | Main product/demo experience. Single-owner plant I/O is useful, but the engine is large and its action queue is unbounded. |
   30 | | `sim_app/` | Separate direct-control sandbox and AI rescue | Useful comparison environment; it intentionally lacks the full SCRAM protections. Emergency-stop precedence needs repair. |
   31 | | `training/`, `model/` | Collection, expert labels, fine-tuning, exported models, evaluations | Reproducible prompt formatting is a strength. Observer validation contamination is confirmed below. |
   32 | | `experiments/` | Adversarial comparisons, frontier sweeps, live rehearsals | Valuable evidence, but recorded results are historical runs rather than validation of this change. |
   33 | | `simulation/`, `packaging/`, `docker/` | Upstream source, image/service integration, visualization | Distinguish local source from the prebuilt image actually executed. |
   34 | | `reference/`, `l1_stub.py`, `run_demo.py` | Older implementation and minimal demo | Keep clearly labeled and remove them from the primary onboarding path. |
   35 | 
   36 | The active control path is `live.Engine → AIOperator → L1Regulator → Keel → L1 signer → PlantService`. The gate checks provenance; the safety layer uses the independent simulated sensor path. Observer telemetry is advisory/display-oriented, while proposal evidence can affect governance. The manual station is a different path and can write directly to the simulator.
   37 | 
   38 | ## Frontend changes delivered
   39 | 
   40 | Both interfaces now share graphite surfaces, mint accents, quieter borders, clearer typography, and responsive layouts. The full control room has a navigation rail on desktop and a compact navigation bar on small screens, distinct overview/console/analysis headings, readable instruments, a defense pipeline, and redesigned valve cards. The manual station places pressure and controls ahead of the large plant viewport and clearly labels its direct-control mode.
   41 | 
   42 | Existing endpoints and control flows are retained. The control-room CSS and JavaScript have been extracted from its monolithic HTML into separate assets. Tab semantics, keyboard arrow/Home/End navigation, a skip link, an accessible command label, and reduced-motion support were added or improved.
   43 | 
   44 | Preview files: [overview](artifacts/frontend/overview-desktop.png), [console](artifacts/frontend/console.png), [analysis](artifacts/frontend/analysis.png), [mobile](artifacts/frontend/overview-390.png), [manual station](artifacts/frontend/studio-desktop.png). These use test telemetry, not live reactor measurements.
   45 | 
   46 | ## Bugs fixed in this change
   47 | 
   48 | | Issue | Previous behavior | Change |
   49 | | --- | --- | --- |
   50 | | Non-finite operator authority | `min(1.0, NaN)` could turn a malformed authority value into full authority. | Reject non-finite values before changing the cap. |
   51 | | Non-finite manual valve input | A NaN/Infinity `value` or `delta` could reach clamping and produce an unintended extreme valve setting. | Reject these at the request-model boundary. Internal direct calls still deserve their own validation. |
   52 | | Stale engine connection status | `Engine.read()` returned the cached healthy snapshot during reconnect, even after `self.status` changed. | Always overlay current engine status/error on the telemetry snapshot. |
   53 | | Premature SIS status | Initial HTML claimed “SIS ARMED” before receiving any state. | Initial/disconnected status is “SIS UNKNOWN.” |
   54 | | Stalled control-room polling | A fetch that never completed stopped subsequent polls. | Five-second request timeout and HTTP-status validation. |
   55 | | Persistent connection warning | A recovered connection could retain its old failure banner. | Clear connection warnings on recovery. |
   56 | | Restarted server lost history/events | Client cursors belonged to the old server sequence and hid new low-numbered events. | Per-engine run identity resets local cursors and cached chart/log state. |
   57 | | Incomplete tab accessibility | Tabs lacked selected state, panel relationships, and expected arrow-key navigation. | Added ARIA relationships, roving focus, and keyboard navigation. |
   58 | | Default pytest collection failed | Pytest imported the root Modbus utility and failed on an optional legacy dependency. | Limit default collection to `tests/` using `pytest.ini`. |
   59 | | A passing test leaked a real connection | The concurrent-reset test's background thread attempted to reconnect to a real simulator, producing an unhandled exception warning. | Mock its post-reset read; verify with thread warnings treated as errors. |
   60 | 
   61 | ## Outstanding bugs and risks, in priority order
   62 | 
   63 | ### High: a low-level trip ignores subsequent overpressure or invalid SIS readings
   64 | 
   65 | In [l0_plant/safety.py](l0_plant/safety.py), `evaluate()` only selects a cause before the initial latch. `safe_state_inputs()` immediately returns `{e_stop: 0, product_valve_sp: 0}` for `level_low`, before checking later pressure or validity. A trip at 4% level followed by 3100 kPa still closes only product and explicitly clears E-stop; a later invalid safety reading behaves the same way. This is reproducible without a simulator.
   66 | 
   67 | Preserve the original trip reason for diagnosis, but evaluate active hazards continuously and apply an explicitly designed priority/escalation policy. Add combined-hazard tests and validate the resulting lineup against the live model. This change deliberately does not invent a new safety-control policy.
   68 | 
   69 | ### High: emergency stop is blocked during AI rescue
   70 | 
   71 | [sim_app/server.py](sim_app/server.py) checks `rescue.active` before permitting manual E-stop, so the request returns HTTP 409. [sim_app/static/app.js](sim_app/static/app.js) also disables the E-stop button while AI control is active. Furthermore, the rescue loop clears simulator E-stop when encountered.
   72 | 
   73 | The emergency-stop action should cancel rescue and take priority over pending AI writes, with one coordinated ownership/locking path. Merely enabling the button is insufficient: test an E-stop while inference is in flight, ensure no later write clears it, and require deliberate release.
   74 | 
   75 | ### High deployment risk: the unauthenticated plant port is published on all host interfaces
   76 | 
   77 | [docker-compose.yml](docker-compose.yml) publishes `55555:55555` and `80:80`. The plant protocol has no authentication and accepts direct writes. The gate can detect/reassert after an out-of-band write, but cannot prevent it. Actual remote reachability depends on host/network firewall rules; external exploitation was not tested.
   78 | 
   79 | For a local-only demo, bind to loopback. For a multi-host lab, use explicit network isolation and writer allowlisting. The fixed demo HMAC keys in `live/engine.py` are also not deployment secrets. These are deliberate demo assumptions that should not be presented as hardened isolation.
   80 | 
   81 | ### Medium: an observer result can survive a reset
   82 | 
   83 | `Observer.reset()` clears history and verdicts, but a pending `_run()` can finish afterward and write the previous run's verdict back into `last`. A controlled delayed response reproduced post-reset suspicion of 0.9. Use a generation identifier captured at dispatch and discard results from older generations. The existing rescue run-ID pattern provides a useful model.
   84 | 
   85 | Related freshness concern: `Governor` expires observer evidence, but `Observer.suspicion()` has no age check and can continue returning an old proposal alarm to other consumers. Apply a shared freshness contract at the observer boundary.
   86 | 
   87 | ### Medium: observer validation contains training prompts
   88 | 
   89 | The checked-in observer v3 data contains **six exact shared user turns** between train and validation: 3,429 unique train turns and 1,195 unique validation turns. The operator dataset has 2,190 unique train turns and 235 unique validation turns, with zero exact overlap.
   90 | 
   91 | `training/build_observer_dataset.py` shuffles a pool of recorded and synthesized windows into train/validation without globally deduplicating that boundary. Its unseen-set filtering only checks against training. Deduplicate before splitting, retain rollout/window provenance, and split by rollout or scenario family with temporal gaps. Rebuild data and rerun evaluation before relying on the existing validation score. The amount by which scores are inflated was not measured.
   92 | 
   93 | ### Medium: bundled C++ source contains an out-of-bounds steady-state read
   94 | 
   95 | `simulation/simulation/TE_process.cc` assigns the purge valve from `b[3]`, outside its three-element solution vector. This is already documented in the repo and partially mitigated by `scripts/reset_plant.py` writing the correct purge setting after restart. The source defect remains.
   96 | 
   97 | Fix and test the actual simulator build, then pin/distribute that image. Editing this local source alone does not update the prebuilt image used by Compose.
   98 | 
   99 | ### Medium: bundled C++ TCP parser does not implement stream framing safely
  100 | 
  101 | In `simulation/simulation/main.cc`, the server reads up to 1,024 bytes into `buffer` and passes it to `reader.parse(buffer, command)` without terminating at `valread` or accumulating complete newline-delimited messages. TCP reads can split or combine messages; the code also does not handle a negative `read()` result separately. Partial `send()` results are ignored. These are source-level defects; the running prebuilt binary was not inspected to establish whether it has identical code.
  102 | 
  103 | Use a bounded per-client receive buffer, parse complete frames by explicit length, handle read/send errors and partial writes, and test fragmented and coalesced requests.
  104 | 
  105 | ### Low: command signing authenticates rounded rather than exact actuator values
  106 | 
  107 | `provenance_gate._tag()` serializes valve values to four decimal places. Changing a signed valve value from 20 to 20.00001 leaves the tag valid and is admitted. The physical change is tiny, but an assertion that every modification is rejected is too strong. Either quantize the command before both signing and applying it, or sign an exact canonical representation.
  108 | 
  109 | ### Documentation and lifecycle gaps
  110 | 
  111 | - The README still leads with `run_demo.py` and the L1 stub. The current product is `python -m live` with `L1Regulator`, Keel, governance, and observers.
  112 | - Composition fields in `PlantState` are documented as mol %, while actual readings are fractions; both regulators now perform the conversion. The README's unresolved conversion item is stale.
  113 | - Architecture text says reset is always deliberate, while the live engine automatically rearms after a clean window with a repeated-trip lockout. Document demo recovery separately from the base interlock contract.
  114 | - `sim_app` starts a perpetual polling thread but does not stop/join it in lifespan shutdown. Repeated app lifecycles in one process can accumulate workers.
  115 | - `live.__main__` can persist a user environment variable and terminate/restart Ollama-related processes on normal launch. Make that an explicit setup operation; `--no-ollama-fix` currently opts out.
  116 | - `requirements.txt` does not provide an installable test dependency set: pytest is missing and httpx is commented out. There is no automated test workflow in `.github/workflows`.
  117 | 
  118 | The first, second, fourth, and signing findings can be reproduced safely with `python -m scripts.review_findings`. That script starts no plant/model services and performs no simulator writes.
  119 | 
  120 | ## Improvements worth prioritizing
  121 | 
  122 | 1. Resolve emergency-stop precedence, secondary-hazard escalation, and stale observer generations. Add race/combined-hazard tests before changing safety behavior.
  123 | 2. Repair dataset separation and rerun held-out evaluation across unseen rollouts, fault severities, and scenario families. Compare the trained operator against both baseline and labeling expert; accurate imitation alone does not demonstrate a better controller.
  124 | 3. Establish a reproducible local environment: development dependencies, a pinned simulator image digest, model/version manifests, and CI for the offline suite plus browser smoke tests.
  125 | 4. Make the active entry point obvious. Consolidate current architecture/recovery documentation and mark historical experiments and stubs explicitly.
  126 | 5. Split `live/engine.py` into orchestration, scenario handling, snapshots, and recovery. Add bounded action queues and observable completion/failure results instead of treating “queued” as completed.
  127 | 6. Track a telemetry timestamp independently of HTTP responsiveness. Retain last-known values for diagnosis but visibly mark them stale, and prevent ordinary commands when the engine cannot execute them reliably.
  128 | 7. Consolidate duplicated design constants and UI styles after the visual direction is accepted. Self-host fonts if offline operation is a requirement. Add chart descriptions and keyboard-accessible numeric summaries for a fuller accessibility pass.
  129 | 
  130 | ## Validation and running the result
  131 | 
  132 | The final offline Python suite passed **249 tests** with background-thread warnings treated as errors. JavaScript syntax checks and `git diff --check` passed. The browser suite covers both applications at desktop and narrow widths, all three control-room tabs, keyboard navigation, chat dispatch, reconnect behavior, server restart recovery, viewport visibility, and horizontal overflow. No browser JavaScript errors were observed in those cases. Initial sandbox runs could not access pytest's temporary folder; the final run used the approved access and completed successfully.
  133 | 
  134 | The two live interlock integration tests were excluded: they reset and manipulate a running GRFICS plant. The Docker simulation, Unity rendering, model inference, and physical recovery traces were not exercised end-to-end for this change. One dependency deprecation warning remains from Starlette's multipart import.
  135 | 
  136 | For the full control room, run `python -m live` and open `http://127.0.0.1:8765`. Its existing defaults may start/reset the simulator and reconfigure Ollama. To attach to an already-running plant without those startup operations, use `python -m live --no-reset --no-ollama-fix --no-browser`. The manual studio is `python -m sim_app` at `http://127.0.0.1:8770`. Avoid operating both writers against the same plant simultaneously.
  137 | 
  138 | Run offline tests with `python -m pytest -q --ignore=tests/test_interlock_truth.py`. Run browser checks with `node tests/frontend_smoke.cjs` after installing Playwright; the script also accepts `PLAYWRIGHT_MODULE` and `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM` paths for an existing installation.

    1 | # Quality improvement pass — 25 October 2026
    2 | 
    3 | This pass improves reliability, dataset integrity, evaluation coverage, and
    4 | telemetry fault detection. It does **not** establish that every AI metric has
    5 | improved. In particular, fresh evaluation exposes an unresolved false-alarm
    6 | problem in the telemetry LLM. No original LLM weights or historical evaluations
    7 | were overwritten, and no model alarms were suppressed to manufacture a score.
    8 | 
    9 | ## Cleanup
   10 | 
   11 | Removed **6,202,172,602 bytes (6.20 GB)** across 16 generated directories:
   12 | two intermediate full-precision observer exports and first-party Python,
   13 | pytest, Ruff, and Unsloth caches. The deployable GGUF models, LoRA adapters,
   14 | checkpoints, training environment, datasets, source, reference material and
   15 | evaluation evidence were retained. Exact paths and sizes are in
   16 | [artifacts/cleanup-manifest.json](artifacts/cleanup-manifest.json).
   17 | 
   18 | The exports can be regenerated from the retained adapters and their base model.
   19 | Ollama uses the GGUF models, not the deleted full-precision exports. The training
   20 | environment is retained because it is useful for reproducible training.
   21 | 
   22 | ## Reliability and control behavior
   23 | 
   24 | - E-stop cancels AI rescue and serializes with valve writes. A model response
   25 |   arriving after cancellation cannot write valves. Rescue no longer releases
   26 |   E-stop; release is deliberate. The UI keeps E-stop available during AI control.
   27 |   A failed stop write remains pending and is reasserted when the connection returns.
   28 | - The safety latch retains the first trip cause while responding to secondary
   29 |   hazards. Combined overpressure/low inventory shuts both feeds, opens purge,
   30 |   and closes product; this avoids the simulator's ordinary E-stop opening the
   31 |   product valve into a low vessel. Safety-sensor loss escalates to latched
   32 |   E-stop. These are explicitly tested simulation policies requiring further
   33 |   physical validation before deployment claims.
   34 | - Observer reset invalidates pending inference generations. Old responses
   35 |   cannot repopulate evidence. Proposal suspicion expires after 30 seconds of
   36 |   control-time age.
   37 | - HMAC signing uses exact canonical float representations. Changes below the
   38 |   former four-decimal rounding precision are now rejected.
   39 | - Plant ports bind to localhost. Runtime signing/logging keys are generated per
   40 |   process unless `SCRAM_L1_KEY`/`SCRAM_KEEL_KEY` are supplied; keys are not printed.
   41 |   The TCP plant protocol itself remains unauthenticated, and same-host/same-process
   42 |   compromise remains outside this boundary.
   43 | - The action queue is bounded at 64 entries and processes at most eight queued
   44 |   actions before another control cycle. HTTP request bodies are bounded at 64 KiB.
   45 | - Telemetry age is exposed independently of HTTP responsiveness; stale telemetry
   46 |   is marked and ordinary frontend controls pause rather than acting on old data.
   47 | - Manual-station polling has an idempotent start and a shutdown/join path.
   48 | - Ordinary startup no longer writes user environment settings or restarts
   49 |   Ollama. Those operations require the explicit `--configure-ollama` option.
   50 | 
   51 | ## Simulator source
   52 | 
   53 | The local C++ source now uses the valid purge-solution element `b[2]`, frees
   54 | steady-state solver buffers, and fixes the delayed-composition loop's swapped
   55 | condition/increment. TCP handling accumulates bounded newline-delimited frames,
   56 | handles fragmented/coalesced requests, rejects invalid input ranges and trailing
   57 | garbage, retries partial writes, and closes excess/oversized connections.
   58 | 
   59 | The source compiled in Ubuntu WSL with `-Wall -Wextra -Werror`. An isolated
   60 | process on a temporary port passed framing, malformed-request, input-bound,
   61 | initial-purge, E-stop and frame-size checks. The app's plant was not reset.
   62 | 
   63 | **Compose still uses the prebuilt GRFICS image.** Source fixes do not silently
   64 | replace its binary or prove equivalence to its extended fault-injection behavior.
   65 | The Python purge workaround remains necessary for that image. Docker Desktop
   66 | was stopped during this pass; full image/Unity/plant rehearsals remain untested.
   67 | 
   68 | ## Clean observer data
   69 | 
   70 | `python -m training.build_clean_observer_dataset` creates versioned inputs under
   71 | `training/observer_clean/`. Entire source recordings are separated before fault
   72 | augmentation, so synthesized children remain with their parent recording.
   73 | 
   74 | - Zero shared user prompts across train, validation and unseen splits.
   75 | - Zero shared selected source recordings across those splits.
   76 | - Exact duplicates are removed, and **477 ambiguous/conflicting user inputs**
   77 |   are excluded rather than teaching different labels for identical telemetry.
   78 | - Pool shortages are reported; validation/test counts are not padded with
   79 |   duplicate examples. The clean splits contain 3,273 / 1,094 / 471 total
   80 |   examples, including proposal examples. Telemetry-only counts are smaller.
   81 | - The manifest records source recordings, class counts, seed, shortages and
   82 |   dataset hashes. Historical v3 files are retained for their existing weights.
   83 | 
   84 | The observer notebook now defaults to clean inputs and a separate candidate
   85 | output directory. Future LLM retraining will therefore not overwrite the
   86 | deployed models by default. This pass trained the CPU specialist below; it did
   87 | not retrain the three existing LLMs.
   88 | 
   89 | ## New advisory telemetry specialist
   90 | 
   91 | A **535 kB CPU ExtraTrees classifier** was trained on 1,796 clean telemetry
   92 | windows. It consumes only measured signals and commanded valve positions.
   93 | The exported JSON forest needs only Python's standard library at runtime;
   94 | NumPy/scikit-learn are training/evaluation dependencies. It adds zero GPU memory.
   95 | 
   96 | Its standalone false-alarm tradeoff failed the desired replacement criteria.
   97 | It is therefore used only for confident sensor/actuator findings when the LLM
   98 | otherwise says normal. On independent validation recordings, that restricted
   99 | policy qualified **99 candidate corrections with zero observed label errors or
  100 | false alarms**, assuming a normal LLM verdict. Actual correction frequency depends
  101 | on the LLM's answers; that validation did not rerun the LLM. The approved model
  102 | digest is checked at load time.
  103 | 
  104 | Corrections retain the original LLM label and identify their source in logs/UI.
  105 | Telemetry judgments remain advisory and do not affect governance authority.
  106 | The proposal path stays on the existing observer v2.
  107 | 
  108 | ### Historical benchmark replay: 480 windows
  109 | 
  110 | This replays saved LLM predictions, so it is development evidence rather than
  111 | a fresh blind evaluation of new LLM weights.
  112 | 
  113 | | Metric | Historical LLM | LLM + restricted specialist |
  114 | | --- | ---: | ---: |
  115 | | Accuracy | 71.46% | **74.17%** |
  116 | | Sensor-fault recall | 21.67% | **32.50%** |
  117 | | Attack/fault detection | 64.72% | **69.17%** |
  118 | | Normal false-alarm rate | 7.50% | **7.50%** |
  119 | | Excursion recall | 99.17% | 99.17% |
  120 | | Actuator-fault recall | 72.50% | 72.50% |
  121 | 
  122 | Some corrections detect an abnormal window but name the wrong fault family;
  123 | those remain classification errors. Full confusion matrices and corrections
  124 | are in [hybrid-evaluation.json](model/telemetry-classifier/hybrid-evaluation.json).
  125 | The standalone candidate's weaker results are retained in
  126 | [evaluation.json](model/telemetry-classifier/evaluation.json).
  127 | 
  128 | ### Fresh local Ollama comparison: 48 balanced clean held-out windows
  129 | 
  130 | The same raw inference response is used for the baseline and corrected result.
  131 | Model IDs, dataset/input hashes, raw responses and timings are stored in
  132 | [artifacts/fresh-observer-benchmark.json](artifacts/fresh-observer-benchmark.json).
  133 | There are only twelve examples per class, so these estimates are uncertain.
  134 | 
  135 | | Metric | Fresh LLM | With specialist |
  136 | | --- | ---: | ---: |
  137 | | Valid structured output | 100% | 100% |
  138 | | Accuracy | 62.50% | **72.92%** |
  139 | | Sensor-fault recall | 50.00% | **91.67%** |
  140 | | Attack/fault detection | 83.33% | **97.22%** |
  141 | | Normal false-alarm rate | **91.67%** | **91.67%** |
  142 | | Excursion recall | 100% | 100% |
  143 | | Actuator-fault recall | 91.67% | 91.67% |
  144 | 
  145 | The high false-alarm rate is a real weakness exposed by the stricter held-out
  146 | recordings. These numbers must not be mixed with the older 480-example sample
  147 | to imply deployment accuracy. The specialist improves missed-fault detection
  148 | without increasing this sample's false alarms, but does not solve them.
  149 | 
  150 | An attempted minimum-effect-size filter would have dismissed three genuine
  151 | sensor faults in validation. It was rejected and is not part of runtime alarm
  152 | handling. More representative benign data, repeated/severity-stratified trials,
  153 | and a separately validated LLM candidate are needed before lowering alarms.
  154 | Operator target errors and other unchanged historical metrics are not claimed
  155 | as improvements.
  156 | 
  157 | ## Verification and reproducibility
  158 | 
  159 | - **271 offline Python tests passed**, with background-thread warnings treated as
  160 |   errors. One dependency deprecation warning remains in Starlette's multipart import.
  161 |   Regression tests cover combined hazards, E-stop during inference,
  162 |   pending-write cancellation, observer reset races, evidence expiry, queue
  163 |   floods, exact signatures, lifecycle shutdown and actual dataset separation.
  164 | - Browser smoke checks cover desktop/tablet/mobile layouts, command dispatch,
  165 |   keyboard navigation, reconnect/restart, stale telemetry, and E-stop access
  166 |   during AI control. No browser JavaScript errors were observed.
  167 | - Linux simulator compilation and isolated protocol checks passed.
  168 | - Added pinned development/evaluation dependencies and GitHub Actions jobs for
  169 |   offline tests, browser checks and simulator compilation/protocol checks.
  170 |   The workflow is configured locally; it has not been run by GitHub in this pass.
  171 | - `README.md` now leads with the current control room, documents units and
  172 |   recovery semantics, and labels historical stubs explicitly.
  173 | 
  174 | Use the commands in [README.md](README.md) to reproduce. JavaScript syntax checks,
  175 | targeted Ruff checks and `git diff --check` also passed. The broader
  176 | `live/engine.py` decomposition and a fully pinned replacement GRFICS image are
  177 | still worthwhile follow-up engineering work.

README.md
Current top-level startup, component map, model setup, verification and limitations entry point.
